q: Which statement about prenatal urinary tract dilation (UTD) is FALSE?
o: VUR accounts for about 10% to 20%
It is found in 1% to 3% of pregnancies
UPJ obstruction is its commonest cause
Most cases are transient (41% to 88%)
e: Transient dilation is the commonest outcome (41–88%); UPJ obstruction is second; VUR 10–20%; others <10%. UTD is the second commonest prenatal finding (1–3% of pregnancies). Screening scan at about 20 weeks; low-risk pregnancies average two scans, high-risk four. Normal APRPD is <7 mm after 28 weeks; 8 mm in the third trimester is low risk (A1). Prenatal detection allows the family to meet a specialist before delivery.

q: Which statement about natural conception is FALSE?
o: About 92% conceive within 12 cycles
Female fecundity falls sharply after 35
About 68% conceive within 3 cycles
Alternate-day intercourse is best
e: Cumulative pregnancy (Gnoth 2003): 38% at 1 cycle, 68% at 3, 81% at 6, 92% at 12 (so about 4/5 by 6 cycles). Daily intercourse around ovulation is likely best (Scarpa 2007), not every other day. In industrialised countries female fecundity declines precipitously after 35.

q: Which statement about ureteral smooth muscle electrophysiology is FALSE?
o: Calcium influx causes the action potential upstroke
Sodium sets the resting membrane potential
Pacemaker cells sit near the pelvicalyceal border
L-type channels carry the inward calcium
e: Resting potential is set mainly by potassium distribution and permeability. On excitation, permeability to K+ falls and Ca2+ (with some Na+) enters through L-type Ca2+ channels, giving the upstroke. Pacemaker cells have less negative resting potentials and lie near the pelvicalyceal border. During development the ureteric lumen obliterates and recanalises; angiotensin via AT2 is involved, and AT2 receptor knockouts get CAKUT (MCDK, megaureter, UPJO).

q: Which statement about urinary incontinence (UI) in men is FALSE?
o: Mixed UI is urgency plus effort leakage
UI is any involuntary loss of urine
Hesitancy is a storage symptom
Stress UI is leakage on effort
e: ICS: UI is any involuntary loss of urine, a storage LUTS. Stress UI: leakage with raised abdominal pressure; urgency UI: with urgency; nocturnal enuresis: during sleep; mixed: urgency and effort; insensible: without awareness. Storage symptoms: frequency, urgency, nocturia, incontinence; hesitancy is a voiding symptom. UI affects up to 39% of men (less than women), harms hygiene and quality of life; type matters for management.

q: Which statement about retropubic suspension surgery is FALSE?
o: Most SUI combines hypermobility with ISD
It works by restoring the normal mechanism
It supports the urethrovesical junction
No standard test separates ISD from mobility
e: Anti-incontinence surgery creates a new, compensatory continence mechanism rather than restoring the original one (Jarvis). It aims to support the urethrovesical junction and correct deficient closure. Hypermobility follows weakening of ligaments, fascia and muscle (ageing, hormones, childbirth, surgery); most women with SUI also have some ISD, with no standard test to split their contributions. Retropubic procedures fix the bladder neck and proximal urethra in a retropubic position.

q: Which statement about intestinal segments is FALSE?
o: Ileum has the most postoperative obstructions
The ileum has a smaller diameter than jejunum
The jejunum has more arcades than ileum
Gastric wedges must never reach the pylorus
e: Ileum: smaller diameter, multiple arcades with smaller vessels; jejunum has fewer arcades. A gastric fundal wedge should not include much antrum and never extend to the pylorus or the full lesser curve. Bowel obstruction after diversion: 4–10%; colon, stomach and sigmoid about 4%, lower than ileum.

q: Which statement about the rationale for focal therapy is FALSE?
o: The index lesion usually sets grade and stage
Gleason 4 and 5 are priority targets
Lethal cancer appears to be monoclonal
Satellites are usually large and high grade
e: Focal therapy assumes the index lesion drives progression: it usually determines grade/stage and most volume; satellites are mostly small (<0.5 mL) and low grade; lethal disease seems monoclonal. Gleason patterns 4 and 5 show malignant hallmarks and are priority targets. Aim: destroy the index lesion while preserving function; success needs a multidisciplinary team, accurate mapping, a compliant patient, complete ablation and monitoring for retreatment or whole-gland conversion. Note: EAU guidelines still regard focal therapy as investigational, best within trials or registries.

q: Which statement about postnatal evaluation of prenatal UTD is FALSE?
o: Fluid shifts can mask dilation at first
The first scan is best within 24 hours
Up to 28% are detected after a normal scan
A normal first scan is repeated in 3–6 months
e: First postnatal US after 48 hours, because early neonatal intravascular depletion (third spacing, later mobilised) can hide dilation. If normal, repeat at 3–6 months: up to 28% appear after an initial negative scan. With no dilation in a circumcised boy, VCUG, prophylaxis and scintigraphy are not warranted.

q: Which drug is NOT a spermatotoxin and may improve semen parameters?
o: Sulfasalazine
Cimetidine
Lisinopril
Spironolactone
e: Lisinopril may improve bulk semen parameters (book). Sulfasalazine causes oligoasthenospermia, reversible on switching to mesalazine. 5α-reductase inhibitors have limited effect on spermatogenesis. Cannabis lowers testosterone; heavy alcohol increases conversion of testosterone to estradiol.

q: Which statement about ureteral smooth muscle contraction is FALSE?
o: Calcium–calmodulin activates MLC kinase
Phospholipase C forms IP3 and DG
Calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Actin phosphorylation triggers contraction
e: Excitation raises sarcoplasmic Ca2+ from 10^-8–10^-7 M to ≥10^-6 M, partly from the endoplasmic/sarcoplasmic reticulum. Ca2+ binds calmodulin; the complex activates myosin light-chain kinase, which phosphorylates the 20-kDa myosin light chain, allowing actin to activate myosin Mg-ATPase. α1-adrenergic and muscarinic agonists activate phospholipase C, hydrolysing PIP2 into IP3 and diacylglycerol (DG); DG activates protein kinase C.

q: Which statement about bowel preparation and perioperative care is FALSE?
o: Mechanical prep can be omitted under ERAS
Mechanical prep lowers bacterial concentration
IV antibiotics belong before the incision
Irradiated bowel causes most lethal complications
e: Mechanical preparation reduces faeces and so the total number of bacteria, not their concentration; antibiotic preparation lowers the concentration. Systemic antibiotics must be given before the operation (about 1 h before incision), and with thromboprophylaxis should never be omitted. Mechanical and oral antibiotic preps and nasogastric tubes are controversial and can be omitted in selected patients (most supporting studies involved isolated anastomoses, not opened bowel); ERAS cystectomy data support omitting mechanical prep. 75% of postoperative deaths related to bowel, 80% of those after prior radiation. Infectious complications occur in up to 10%. Without NG tubes, major complications are no different but distension, nausea and vomiting are commoner.

q: Which statement about imaging and biopsy for focal therapy is FALSE?
o: Systematic biopsy is still needed with MRI
TRUS biopsy misses about 30% of significant cancers
mpMRI misses 10% to 15% of significant cancers
mpMRI accurately sizes the tumour
e: mpMRI underestimates tumour volume by 5–30% on whole-mount correlation, so margins matter. TRUS biopsy overdiagnoses insignificant cancer, misses about 30% of significant cancers (anterior/apical), under-represents burden and is inconsistent on repeat. mpMRI preferentially detects high-grade, anterior and extraprostatic disease and targets the index lesion, but misses 10–15%, so systematic biopsy is still required. Multiparametric US and PSMA PET are under evaluation.

q: Which statement about fetal intervention for lower urinary tract obstruction (LUTO) is FALSE?
o: Fetal cystoscopy can diagnose and treat valves
Oligohydramnios before 27 weeks is a poor sign
It reliably preserves long-term renal function
It appears to improve perinatal survival
e: Prenatal LUTO intervention improves survival without a reliable effect on long-term renal function; it helps most with oligohydramnios early in the second trimester (lung development after 27 weeks). Poor predictors: oligohydramnios before 27 weeks, renal cortical cysts, increased echogenicity. Fetal cystoscopy can diagnose and treat; it may give short-term renal benefit over vesicoamniotic shunting, but long-term data are lacking. US correlates best with obstructive lesions (UPJO, PUV) and less with VUR.

q: Which statement about testicular injury is FALSE?
o: Testicular doses of 7.5 Gy lower fatherhood
11% develop antisperm antibodies after torsion
Scrotal temperature equals core temperature
Sperm DNA damage may last 2 years after chemo
e: A vascular heat exchanger and muscle activity keep the scrotum 2–4°C below core. Fatherhood probability falls significantly at testicular doses ≥7.5 Gy, even without direct exposure. DNA damage may be detectable up to 2 years after chemotherapy. 11% develop antisperm antibodies after torsion. Low concentrations of most bacteria (including E. coli) have little effect on motility: observe. HIV has no clear direct effect on sperm function.

q: Which is NOT part of the initial assessment of a man with UI?
o: Frequency-volume chart
Flow test
Urinalysis
Invasive urodynamics
e: Baseline: flow test, bladder diary/frequency-volume chart, urinalysis (infection, blood) and a quality-of-life questionnaire. Invasive urodynamics (filling cystometry, pressure-flow) only after failed conservative and medical therapy and when it will change management. Risk factors: age, infection, functional/cognitive impairment, neurological disease, diabetes, prostatectomy, drugs, alcohol; race and ethnicity were not significant. Treatment is usually conservative and medical first, with surgery for failures with QoL impact.

q: Which statement about ureteral relaxation is FALSE?
o: Guanylyl cyclase degrades cyclic GMP
Phosphodiesterases break down cAMP and cGMP
Nitric oxide raises cGMP to relax muscle
cAMP mediates β-adrenergic relaxation
e: Cyclic AMP mediates β-agonist relaxation (isoproterenol depresses contractility). cGMP is made from GTP by guanylyl cyclase (activated by nitric oxide) and degraded to 5'-GMP by phosphodiesterase; phosphodiesterases degrade both nucleotides and can be selectively inhibited. NOS converts L-arginine to NO and L-citrulline (NADPH-dependent); inducible NOS is NADPH-dependent and calcium-independent. PDE inhibitors and α1A antagonists relax the ureter.

q: Which statement about conservative behavioural treatment of incontinence is FALSE?
o: It suits young women with SUI alone
It is recommended first-line by guidelines
It needs an active, motivated patient
Intensive clinician-led programmes do better
e: Behavioural treatments change behaviour or environment or teach skills; strong evidence supports them as first-line for stress, urgency and mixed UI and OAB in men and women of any age, and they are essentially risk-free. Bladder training is patient-dependent (education, incremental voiding schedules, urge control) and needs function, learning capability and motivation. Intensive programmes with an experienced clinician are more effective.

q: Which statement about defining and assessing SUI before colposuspension is FALSE?
o: About 40% of fit nulliparae leak with exercise
Urodynamic SUI needs a detrusor contraction
Prior failed surgery lowers Burch success
Patient-reported outcomes are the key end point
e: ICS urodynamic SUI: leakage with raised abdominal pressure during filling cystometry without detrusor contraction; whether urodynamics is needed for successful treatment is unclear. Burch success: 81% after one failed repair, 25% after two, 0% after three (Petrou), though other series show good repeat results. Trials should use validated symptom and QoL instruments; pressure-flow studies are not justified routinely. About 40% of nulliparous women aged 30–49 leak with exercise. ISD: leak point pressure <60 cmH2O or MUCP <20 cmH2O.

q: Which pairing of bowel segment and metabolic disorder is FALSE?
o: Ureterosigmoidostomy: marked hypokalaemia
Jejunum: hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis
Stomach: hypochloraemic alkalosis too
Ileum or colon: hyperchloraemic acidosis
e: Jejunum: hyperkalaemic, hyponatraemic metabolic acidosis. Ileum and colon: hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, sometimes with potassium deficiency; segments retain this ability over time. Stomach: hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis (the only alkalosis; arginine hydrochloride has no role in acidosis from other segments) and haematuria-dysuria syndrome; severe alkalosis occurs with high gastrin, dehydration and failure to empty the pouch. Hypokalaemia and total body potassium depletion are commonest with ureterosigmoidostomy.

q: Which statement about prostate cryotherapy is FALSE?
o: A urethral warmer cuts urethral injury
A nadir of −40°C is needed for cell death
Double freeze–thaw cycles are recommended
Rapid thawing kills more cells than slow
e: Cell destruction depends on cooling rate, warming rate and nadir temperature; slow thawing is more destructive. Complete death is unlikely above −20°C; −40°C or lower is needed; repeat freeze/thaw adds damage; heat sinks matter. Mechanisms: intra- and extracellular ice, recrystallisation, vascular stasis, apoptosis, immune effects. Advances: real-time TRUS, urethral warming catheter, thermocouples, percutaneous fine (17 G third-generation) probes and variable ice length. On US the frozen zone is hypoechoic with a hyperechoic rim and shadowing; US shows no temperature and not the lateral/anterior extent. (Neurovascular bundle warming is not one of these advances.)

q: Which statement about postnatal UTD risk categories is FALSE?
o: P1 UTD needs prophylaxis and a VCUG
P2 includes APD ≥15 mm or peripheral calyces
P3 UTD needs prophylaxis, VCUG and MAG3
P3 adds parenchymal or bladder abnormality
e: UTD system combines APD and SFU grades, adds the lower tract and gives standard reporting and risk stratification. P1 (low risk; book: SFU 2, APD 10–<15 mm): no prophylaxis or VCUG; most resolve within 30 months (complete resolution by about 4 years). P2 (intermediate; APD ≥15 mm, peripheral calyceal or ureteral dilation): prophylaxis and VCUG at the clinician's discretion. P3 (high): plus abnormal parenchymal thickness/appearance or bladder: US at 1 month, VCUG, prophylaxis, MAG3 at discretion. SFU grading is a five-point (0–4) system based on calyceal dilation and parenchyma.

q: In an obese infertile man, the expected hormone pattern is:
o: High testosterone, high SHBG, low estradiol
Low testosterone, low SHBG, high estradiol
Normal testosterone, low SHBG, low estradiol
Low testosterone, high SHBG, low estradiol
e: Obesity lowers testosterone; SHBG falls (probably from high insulin); estradiol rises from aromatase in excess adipose tissue. By contrast, ageing raises SHBG and lowers bioavailable testosterone.

q: A woman with urgency is taught urge suppression. When urgency strikes she should:
o: Strain gently to empty the bladder at once
Hurry to the nearest toilet before leaking
Drink less fluid for the rest of the day
Sit, squeeze pelvic floor, then walk
e: Rushing raises bladder pressure and fullness, worsens urgency and can trigger detrusor contraction; toilet cues add urgency. Stay away from the toilet, pause, sit, relax, contract the pelvic floor repeatedly until the urge passes, then walk at normal pace. A bladder diary records fluid intake, voids, urgency and leaks, plans therapy and is the best noninvasive way to monitor it.

q: Which statement about urine transport is FALSE?
o: Contraction must exceed bladder pressure
Resting ureteral pressure is 20–80 cmH2O
Bladder pressure >40 cmH2O decompensates it
Bolus transport needs full wall coaptation
e: Resting ureteral pressure is 0–5 cmH2O; contractions reach 20–80 cmH2O. The wave starts proximally, coapts the walls and pushes a bolus distally; contractile pressure must exceed intravesical pressure to cross the UVJ, so storage-phase bladder pressure is paramount; sustained pressures >40 cmH2O cause ureteral decompensation. Laplace: pressure = (tension × wall thickness)/radius, so tension = (pressure × radius)/thickness. Hysteresis: at a given length, resting force is lower and contractile force higher when shortening than when stretched (viscoelastic).

q: Which statement about stomas and ureterointestinal anastomoses is FALSE?
o: Loop end ileostomy suits obese patients
Refluxing anastomoses stricture more often
Stomas go through the rectus belly
Wallace anastomosis has the fewest strictures
e: Antirefluxing anastomoses stricture in 10–20%, refluxing in 3–10%; Wallace has the lowest rate. Strictures away from the anastomosis are commonest on the left where the ureter crosses the aorta under the IMA. Stomas go through the belly of rectus, at the peak of the infraumbilical fat roll; loop end ileostomy is easier in obese patients. Absorbable sutures/staples are preferred where bowel meets urine (non-absorbable ones are less compatible).

q: Which statement about fetal myelomeningocele closure (MOMS trial, 2011) is FALSE?
o: Counselling should be at a fetal centre
It reduces the need for VP shunting
It improves motor and cognitive outcomes
It improves urodynamics and avoids CIC
e: The 2011 randomised trial of prenatal versus postnatal closure showed less ventriculoperitoneal shunting and better motor and cognitive function, but no improvement in urodynamic parameters or the need for CIC or reconstruction. Counsel at a centre with fetal surgery expertise and a multidisciplinary team.

q: An azoospermic man has FSH 10 IU/L and testis long axis 4.3 cm. Most likely cause and next step:
o: Testicular failure; micro-TESE
Obstruction; vasoepididymostomy now
Hypogonadism; testosterone therapy
Obstruction; transrectal ultrasound
e: Schoor: FSH ≤7.6 IU/L and long axis >4.6 cm gives 96% probability of obstruction; FSH >7.6 and axis ≤4.6 cm gives 89% probability of spermatogenic dysfunction. Long axis ≤4.6 cm (caliper) is associated with impaired spermatogenesis; testis size correlates with sperm production. Spermatogenesis may be focal, so random biopsy can miss sperm: microdissection TESE. With normal FSH and examination and no dilated seminal vesicles (ejaculatory duct obstruction unlikely), do sperm retrieval with cryopreservation.

q: Which statement about the Burch colposuspension is FALSE?
o: Sutures pass through the pubic symphysis
It lifts the vagina toward Cooper ligament
It needs adequate vaginal mobility
Opening the bladder may aid dissection
e: Burch: two to four sutures each side elevate the anterior vaginal wall and paravesical tissue to the iliopectineal (Cooper) ligament; needs adequate vaginal mobility and capacity. Vagino-obturator shelf anchors to obturator internus fascia. MMK places sutures in the symphysis periosteum, risking osteitis pubis (0.9–3.2%; pain at 1–8 weeks radiating to thighs; rest, analgesia, steroids). Position supine/low lithotomy with vaginal access; Foley balloon locates bladder neck; Pfannenstiel or midline; opening the bladder may help. Burch is the standard open retropubic procedure; MMK, paravaginal repair and needle suspensions are not recommended.

q: Which statement about focal ablation energies is FALSE?
o: IRE is a non-thermal, pore-forming method
HIFU kills by coagulative necrosis ≥55°C
Laser ablation acts within a fixed distance
HIFU treats anterior lesions most easily
e: HIFU focuses beams to ≥55°C causing coagulative necrosis; the transrectal transducer suits posterior lesions; anterior targets are harder (energy dissipation, oedema displacing targets). New: in-bore MRgFUS and MRI-guided transurethral ultrasound ablation (TULSA). Focal laser ablation: interstitial fibre, necrosis within a fixed distance, safe near vital structures; larger lesions need longer time or more fibres and margins need care. IRE: short DC pulses create irreversible membrane pores, sparing connective tissue scaffolding. Patterns: hemi-, quadrant- or lesion-ablation. Brachytherapy, SBRT, toxins and nanoparticles are under study.

q: Which statement about UTI risk and prophylaxis in prenatal UTD is FALSE?
o: Higher-grade dilation raises UTI risk
Meta-analysis proved prophylaxis works
Intact foreskin is a UTI risk factor
UTI incidence in UTD is about 8% to 19%
e: An 11-study meta-analysis showed no benefit of continuous prophylaxis; UTI incidence is low (8–19%), so studies are hard. Degree of dilation predicts UTI risk; risk factors: female sex, intact foreskin, high-grade dilation, ureteral dilation, VUR. Book: prophylaxis for P2 and P3. Boy with P2 UTD, ureteral dilation and intact foreskin: discuss and recommend newborn circumcision; keep prophylaxis; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole not before 2–3 months. VCUG decisions are based on UTI risk unless LUTO is suspected.

q: According to the book, which statement about semen analysis is FALSE?
o: Brown semen is seen in cord injury
Normal semen volume is 1 to 5 mL
Progressive motility is 32% to 63%
Seven days' abstinence is optimal
e: Book: a single day of abstinence is optimal for bulk parameters; normal volume 1–5 mL; progressive motility 32–63%; ejaculate normally white/grey, brown in spinal cord injury. Update: WHO (2010 and 2021 manuals) advises 2–7 days of abstinence; WHO 2021 lower reference limits are volume 1.4 mL, concentration 16 million/mL, progressive motility 30%, normal forms 4%. Spermatogenesis takes about 64 days (some newer estimates ~74) plus 5–10 days of epididymal transit.

q: Which statement about ureteral innervation is FALSE?
o: Autonomic transmitters drive peristalsis
α stimulation increases ureteral activity
Peristalsis continues without innervation
The ureter is syncytial with no true NMJs
e: Tetrodotoxin and autonomic blockers barely affect peristalsis: autonomic transmitters play little role, though sympathetic input modulates it. Peristalsis persists without nerves; the ureter is syncytial smooth muscle without discrete neuromuscular junctions; fibres are longitudinal, circular and spiral. α-adrenergic stimulation increases, β inhibits activity. Norepinephrine is made from tyrosine; reuptake ends its action; cocaine and imipramine block reuptake and potentiate it. Tachykinins excite; CGRP inhibits. Prostaglandins come from arachidonic acid via COX-1/COX-2.

t: UUI and SUI drugs in men
q: Which statement about drug treatment of incontinence is FALSE?
o: Botulinum toxin follows failed first line
Duloxetine is licensed for female SUI
Antimuscarinics are licensed for SUI
IPSS does not ask about incontinence
e: First-line UUI: bladder training, pelvic floor training, antimuscarinics; then intradetrusor botulinum toxin A. Antimuscarinics are licensed for OAB, not SUI. Duloxetine (SNRI) is licensed (in Europe) for female SUI, not UUI. IPSS/AUA-SI asks three storage (urgency, frequency, nocturia), three voiding (intermittency, weak stream, straining) and one post-micturition question (incomplete emptying), but not incontinence.

q: Which statement about renal function and continent diversion is FALSE?
o: A GFR over 60 mL/min is required
Urine osmolality ≥600 on deprivation
Serum creatinine reflects GFR well
Urine pH of 5.8 or less is required
e: Urea and creatinine are reabsorbed by ileum and colon, so serum values overstate function, more so in continent diversions. For a retentive diversion: urine pH ≤5.8, osmolality ≥600 mOsm/kg with water deprivation, GFR >60 mL/min and minimal proteinuria. Long-term, 20% of renal units deteriorate significantly. After >15 years, ureterosigmoidostomy deaths are mainly from renal disease (sepsis, renal failure).

q: Which statement about vascular-targeted photodynamic therapy (VTP) is FALSE?
o: It uses near-infrared light and a photosensitiser
It damages membranes and small arterioles
It showed no benefit over surveillance
Progression was 28% versus 58% on surveillance
e: VTP: intravascular photosensitiser plus low-power near-infrared laser creates reactive oxygen species, damaging membranes and small arterioles. PCM301 (Azzouzi 2017): 415 men with low-risk cancer randomised to VTP or AS; VTP improved negative biopsy at 2 years and reduced progression (28% vs 58%) and need for radical therapy; first level 1 evidence for focal therapy. Note: padeliporfin (TOOKAD) is approved in Europe but not by the US FDA.

q: Which statement about neonatal urological problems is FALSE?
o: MCDK does not increase Wilms tumour risk
Bilateral impalpable testes need CAH testing
Mesoblastic nephroma raises Wilms risk later
Neonatal renal tumours are uncommon
e: Congenital mesoblastic nephroma is the commonest (though uncommon) neonatal renal tumour. MCDK does not increase Wilms risk and can usually be observed. A 'boy' with bilateral impalpable testes or ambiguous genitalia needs electrolytes to exclude salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Abdominal distension: urinary ascites, obstruction, renal mass, rarely adrenal mass. Retention: LUTO (PUV in boys; UG sinus or cloaca in girls). Neonatal gross haematuria: urinalysis and Doppler US. (The book's next outline lists chapters 23–27: evaluation of the child, imaging, infection, perioperative care, laparoscopy.)

q: Which pairing of semen problem and test is FALSE?
o: Total immotility: immunobead test first
DNA fragmentation: TUNEL assay test
Leucocytes vs germ cells: Papanicolaou
IVF ability: hamster egg penetration
e: With complete asthenospermia, exclude necrospermia first with a vital stain; immunobead antisperm antibody testing needs some motile sperm. If sperm are alive but immotile, electron microscopy shows ultrastructural tail defects (immotile cilia). Papanicolaou separates leucocytes from immature germ cells. Direct DNA fragmentation: TUNEL and neutral comet. The sperm penetration assay uses zona-free hamster ova. Low volume: first a post-ejaculate urinalysis (retrograde ejaculation); other causes are ejaculatory duct obstruction and accessory gland hypoplasia.

q: Which advice for a patient with urgency and frequency is FALSE?
o: Try stopping caffeine for 3 to 5 days
Use a diary to find irritant drinks
Drink about 30 mL/kg spread across the day
Restrict fluids well below 1 L daily
e: Review a 24–48 h intake/output diary for excess, inadequate or badly timed intake. Encourage normal hydration (about six 8-oz glasses, ~30 mL/kg/day, at least 1500 mL) at set times unless medically contraindicated; dehydration concentrates urine and worsens urgency. A food/drink diary with one-at-a-time elimination confirms irritants; a 3–5 day caffeine-free trial often persuades patients. Teach pelvic floor contraction correctly first; good results with 45–60 paired contractions/relaxations daily; teach urethral occlusion ('the knack') before leakage triggers.

q: Which is a contraindication to Burch colposuspension?
o: Inadequate vaginal length or mobility
Concurrent laparotomy for other surgery
Limited vaginal access for a sling
Chronic cough with hypermobility
e: Indications for a retropubic approach include laparotomy for other abdominal surgery and limited vaginal access; chronic cough or strenuous work may favour it or a sling. Contraindications: significant sphincter deficiency (suspect after prior failures; a fascial sling is preferred when ISD is primary), MUCP <20 cmH2O, pan-pelvic floor weakness and inadequate vaginal length/mobility; it may not correct coexisting prolapse.

q: Which statement about the ureter in disease is FALSE?
o: Pregnancy hydroureter is mainly hormonal
Infection reduces ureteral contractions
Obstruction lengthens and widens the ureter
Progesterone inhibits ureteral activity
e: Obstruction of pregnancy is mainly mechanical, secondarily hormonal: progesterone inhibits ureteral function, increases dilatation and delays postpartum resolution. Infection reduces contractions and UVJ compliance, permitting reflux. Obstruction gradually increases ureteral length and diameter. UPJO may be anatomic or due to disordered peristalsis (altered muscle configuration). Stone passage is helped by higher proximal hydrostatic pressure and relaxation at the stone; indomethacin reduces pelvic pressure and wall tension, easing colic. c-KIT positive cells are needed for unidirectional peristalsis; pacemaker conduction uses L-type Ca2+ channels amplified by prostanoids, opposed by K+ channels.

q: Which statement about long-term effects of urinary diversion is FALSE?
o: Detubularised bowel holds less volume
Diversion in children can limit growth
Ureterosigmoidostomy has the highest cancer risk
Osteomalacia is linked to persistent acidosis
e: Reconfiguring (detubularising) bowel usually increases volume; long-term effects on motor activity and wall tension are unclear. Cancer risk is highest where urothelium meets colonic epithelium bathed in faeces (ureterosigmoidostomy). Diversion can limit linear growth. Osteomalacia: persistent acidosis, vitamin D resistance and renal calcium loss, commoner with persistent hyperchloraemic acidosis. Ileal conduit is the simplest with the fewest early complications; transverse colon is used when pelvic bowel is irradiated.

q: Which statement about follow-up after focal therapy is FALSE?
o: mpMRI is repeated at 1–2 and 5 years
Systematic biopsy checks the untreated zone
PSA alone reliably shows treatment success
Biopsy the treated zone at 3–6 months
e: PSA is less useful because residual gland keeps producing it. ICUD 2015: mpMRI with mandatory 4–6 core targeted biopsy of the treated zone at 3–6 months; mpMRI at 1–2 and 5 years with targeted biopsy as needed; systematic biopsy at 1–2 and 5 years for outfield recurrence. Future work: better selection (imaging, genetic biomarkers), cost-effectiveness and adjuvant agents.

q: A newborn's scrotal examination changes acutely on day 2 with a new tender swelling. The best management is:
o: Observation until 6 months
Scrotal Doppler next week
Emergency exploration
Serial scrotal examinations
e: An acute postnatal change means postnatal torsion: up to 44% can be salvaged by emergency exploration and septopexy; Doppler only if the diagnosis is unclear and should not delay surgery. Prenatal torsion: unchanged from birth, hard nontender mass with no flow, not salvageable; most perform urgent contralateral septopexy. Acuity dictates urgency.

q: Which statement about genetic male infertility is FALSE?
o: ΔF508 is the commonest CFTR mutation
Test genetics if density <5 million/mL
AZFc deletions abolish sperm output
Klinefelter is the commonest genetic cause
e: AZF is on Yq; DAZ genes lie in AZFc. AZFc microdeletion may impair but not abolish spermatogenesis (sperm often retrievable); AZFa and AZFb deletions generally mean no spermatogenesis. Klinefelter (47,XXY) is the commonest genetic cause. Consider genetic testing for spermatogenic azoospermia or density <5 million/mL. Congenital bilateral absence of the vas: test for CFTR (ΔF508 is commonest and severe), test the partner (child could have CF via ICSI), and do renal ultrasound (agenesis in 11%).

q: Which statement about voiding difficulty after colposuspension is FALSE?
o: Most cases reflect detrusor failure
Over-tight or medial sutures can cause it
Warn every patient about possible CISC
It is likelier with preexisting dysfunction
e: Postoperative voiding difficulty is commoner with preexisting detrusor dysfunction or denervation, but most often reflects overcorrection by misplaced or over-tight sutures; medial sutures can transfix or distort the urethra. Counsel all patients about possible self-catheterisation. Other complications: bleeding (transfusion 3–8%), organ injury, infection, VTE, de novo DO, prolapse. Voiding symptoms with new irritative symptoms and a retropubically angulated urethra suggest obstruction. Preexisting DO (up to 30%) does not contraindicate surgery if anatomic SUI is shown; it usually resolves.

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: Bilateral undescended testes need orchidopexy
Pre-Seed spares sperm motility
Varicoceles occur in 30–50% of infertile men
Saliva is a sperm-safe lubricant
e: Nearly all lubricants, including saliva, are spermatotoxic; Pre-Seed did not reduce motility or chromatin integrity. Adult with bilateral distal cryptorchidism: orchidopexy removes the spermatotoxic insult (no benefit from waiting; biopsy unnecessary). Varicocele: 15% of men, 30–50% of those with infertility. Antisperm antibodies follow vasectomy, testis trauma, orchitis, cryptorchidism, testis cancer and varicocele; Sertoli cell tight junctions protect haploid gametes.

q: Which statement about prolapse and colposuspension is FALSE?
o: Prophylactic hysterectomy improves results
Burch can predispose to enterocele
Non-absorbable sutures can enter the bladder
Burch at sacrocolpopexy cuts later SUI
e: Prolapse follows Burch in about 22% (9.5–38%); lateral vaginal elevation aggravates posterior weakness, causing enterocele in 3–17%, so cul-de-sac obliteration is sometimes added. Simultaneous hysterectomy does not improve outcome; do it only for uterine pathology. Adding Burch to abdominal sacrocolpopexy substantially reduces later SUI in continent women (CARE trial). Non-absorbable sutures may migrate into the bladder and form stones or infection.

q: Which statement about endocrine causes of male infertility is FALSE?
o: Abrupt right varicocele needs renal imaging
Androgen insensitivity gives low testosterone
A mildly raised prolactin should be repeated
Anosmia with low gonadotropins is Kallmann
e: Androgen receptor insensitivity: raised testosterone and estradiol, variably raised LH, normal FSH. Kallmann syndrome: hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia, confirmed by a smell test. Prolactin is labile: confirm moderate rises. Solitary right varicocele is rare; abrupt onset suggests renal pathology (renal ultrasound).

q: In the SISTEr trial (Albo 2007), compared with Burch colposuspension, the autologous fascial sling gave:
o: Higher success with more adverse events
Lower success with fewer adverse events
Equal success with fewer voiding problems
Lower success and more serious adverse events
e: 655 women randomised; at 24 months success was higher with the sling (overall 47% vs 38%; SUI-specific 66% vs 49%); serious adverse events similar (13% vs 10%), but more total adverse events and more voiding dysfunction with the sling. Laparoscopic colposuspension: better view, less pain, shorter stay, faster recovery, but harder, longer and costlier (Tan 2007 meta-analysis). Note: midurethral slings are now the usual first-line surgery for SUI.

q: Which pairing of sperm abnormality and management is FALSE?
o: Macrocephalic multi-tailed sperm: ICSI
Isolated low morphology: reassurance
Globozoospermia: ICSI with ejaculated sperm
T6 cord injury ejaculation: give nifedipine
e: Macrocephaly with multiple tails has high aneuploidy, so ICSI with his sperm is not advised; use donor sperm (IUI). Globozoospermia (no acrosome, round heads) cannot fertilise naturally or by conventional IVF: ICSI, with ejaculated sperm if present. Varied abnormal forms with otherwise normal parameters: likely over-reading; reassure. Ejaculatory stimulation at or above T6 risks autonomic dysreflexia: nifedipine beforehand and BP monitoring. IUI is unlikely below 13.5 million/mL and favourable above 48 million/mL (Guzick).

q: Which statement about anteroposterior diameter (APD) is FALSE?
o: Greater dilation means more urologic disease
APD relates linearly to obstruction
Third-trimester APD of 15 mm predicts surgery
APD correlates closely with grade of VUR
e: APD correlates poorly with the presence and grade of VUR. It relates linearly to obstructive lesions (UPJO, PUV); third-trimester APD of 15 mm has reasonable positive predictive value for UPJO surgery. Book: an 'inverse relationship' between UTD severity and incidence of disease; in practice, the more severe the dilation, the likelier significant pathology. VUR in up to 31% of screened UTD, commonest in boys, bilateral and high grade.

q: Which statement about duplication and megaureter is FALSE?
o: Lower pole VUR can alter upper pole plans
Repair for recurrent UTI or falling function
Under age 1, temporary diversion is preferred
Most primary megaureters need early repair
e: Most primary megaureters resolve spontaneously; operate for recurrent UTI, falling function or increasing dilation, with temporising diversion under 1 year. In duplication, lower pole VUR may influence management of an obstructed upper pole. MAG3 surgical indications (Sussman): differential function <40%, T½ >20 min, retention on upright delayed images. MAG3 is tubular (not GFR), affected by hydration, gives poor anatomy (MR urography best for ectopic insertion); furosemide timing is individualised.

q: Which is NOT a recognised risk factor for UI in men?
o: Cognitive impairment
Race or ethnicity
Neurological disease
Prior prostatectomy
e: Race and ethnicity were not statistically significant. Risk factors: age, urological infection, neurological and cognitive impairment, prostatectomy, diabetes, drugs and alcohol.

q: A ureteral stricture away from the ureterointestinal anastomosis is most often found:
o: Left side, at the ureterovesical end
Right side, beside the duodenum
Right side, near the pelvic brim area
Left side, where it crosses the aorta
e: The left ureter is tunnelled under the sigmoid mesentery and crosses the aorta beneath the IMA, where it may be devascularised or angulated.

q: Omitting nasogastric decompression after urinary diversion mainly leads to:
o: More anastomotic leaks from bowel
More wound dehiscence and hernias
More ileus needing reoperation
More distension and vomiting
e: Major intestinal complications did not differ with or without NG tubes; patients without them had more distension, nausea and vomiting.

q: By the Laplace relation, ureteral wall tension equals:
o: Radius × wall thickness ÷ pressure
Pressure ÷ (radius × wall thickness)
Pressure × wall thickness ÷ radius
Pressure × radius ÷ wall thickness
e: Pressure = (tension × wall thickness)/radius. So for a given tension, a dilated ureter (larger radius) generates lower intraluminal pressure.

q: A man has low semen volume. The first test should be:
o: Seminal vesiculography
Transrectal ultrasound scan
Testicular biopsy now
Post-ejaculate urine test
e: It is the simplest, least invasive way to exclude retrograde ejaculation; the other causes are ejaculatory duct obstruction and accessory gland hypoplasia.

q: A normal renal pelvic APD after 28 weeks' gestation is less than:
o: 7 mm
15 mm
12 mm
4 mm
e: After 28 weeks, APRPD <7 mm is normal; 8 mm is low-risk (A1) dilation; postnatal US after 48 hours.

q: On transrectal ultrasound during cryotherapy, the frozen zone appears as:
o: Hypoechoic with a hyperechoic rim
Hyperechoic with a hypoechoic rim
Anechoic with posterior enhancement
Isoechoic and poorly marginated
e: Ice differs in acoustic impedance, giving a bright, well-defined leading edge with shadowing; US does not show temperature or the lateral/anterior extent.

q: A girl with gastrocystoplasty has severe vomiting and lethargy. The most likely disorder is:
o: Hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis
Hyperkalaemic metabolic acidosis
Hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis
Hypermagnesaemic respiratory acidosis
e: Stomach secretes acid: hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic alkalosis, worst with high gastrin, dehydration and poor pouch emptying. Haematuria-dysuria syndrome is the other stomach-specific problem.

q: Which statement about pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) is FALSE?
o: One exact exercise regimen is proven best
45–60 contractions a day gave good results
Check correct contraction before starting
Teach contraction just before a cough
e: The ideal regimen is not known; trials with 45–60 paired contractions and relaxations daily did well, often written as an 'exercise prescription'. Verify correct identification and contraction first. Teach patients to occlude the urethra by contracting before coughing or lifting.

q: Which statement about choosing a focal ablation technology is FALSE?
o: Operator experience affects the choice
One energy source suits any lesion
Choice depends on lesion location
Delivering a lethal dose is the goal
e: Choice depends on availability, operator experience, approach and the ability to deliver a lethal dose to the location; patterns include hemi-, quadrant- and lesion-ablation.

q: Which agent depresses ureteral smooth muscle contractility?
o: Bethanechol
Substance P
Isoproterenol
Phenylephrine
e: Isoproterenol (β agonist) relaxes via cAMP. α agonists (phenylephrine), cholinergic agonists and tachykinins such as substance P increase activity; CGRP inhibits.

q: Which statement about UI in men is TRUE?
o: Its subtypes need no differentiation
It can affect up to 39% of men
It is commoner in men than women
Surgery is first-line for most men
e: UI is less prevalent in men than women but can reach 39%; distinguishing SUI, UUI, mixed and other types guides care; conservative and medical therapy come first.

q: Which statement about conservative incontinence care is TRUE?
o: It carries a high complication rate
It works only with a clinician present
It is reserved for after drug failure
It relies on patient effort
e: Behavioural therapy is patient-dependent, essentially risk-free and first-line; clinician-led intensive programmes are more effective, but patients do the work.
